name: Extreme dieting / low body fat

lead: Leanmaxxing means sustained calorie deficits to reach very low body fat, with forum targets of about 10 to 15%, aiming for a sharper jaw, visible cheekbones and defined muscle. Members disagree on the ideal level, and some report their face stayed full even when lean.

A sustained energy deficit reduces fat stores across the body, and where fat leaves first varies by person. Sports-science reviews describe how bodybuilders and weight-class athletes diet for contests, including higher protein intake during deficits, and typically hold extreme leanness only briefly.

paras: People run a long calorie deficit, often with high protein and resistance training to hold muscle, and track weight and photos over months. Competitors in physique sports hold peak leanness only for the contest period.

The IOC and the RED-S literature document hormonal, bone, mood and performance problems from prolonged low energy availability in men and women, including lower androgen levels, bone density and strength in men. Disordered eating is a recognised concern in weight-sensitive sports.

web.title: Why young men are starvemaxxing (Business Insider via Yahoo)
Facial Adiposity, Attractiveness, and Health: A Review

angle.text: Leanmaxxing means a prolonged calorie deficit to reach roughly 10 to 15% body fat, which reveals the jaw, cheekbones and muscle definition. Facial fat distribution is partly genetic, so how much the face changes varies, and sports medicine documents the practice in competition prep.

lead: Extreme dieting to low body fat is the practice of sustained, aggressive calorie restriction aimed at a very lean physique. In looksmaxxing communities it is called leanmaxxing, cutting or shredding, and sometimes by the more extreme label "starvemaxxing". The appearance goal is facial and bodily definition: less fat over the cheeks and under the jaw, a sharper jawline, visible cheekbones, and visible abdominal and shoulder muscle.[1][2][3] Members usually pair it with resistance training so that the leanness reveals muscle rather than replacing it.[2][4]

How lean is lean enough is argued constantly. Forum members typically name targets between about 10 and 15 percent body fat, with some saying that going lower makes the face look better and others saying that past a certain point the face stays the same and only the body shrinks.[2][5][6] Several threads ask why a very lean body can coexist with a fuller face, which posters usually attribute to genetics and bone structure.[1][6][7]

The wider literature on the subject comes mostly from sports and nutrition science. Reviews describe how competitive bodybuilders and weight-class athletes diet before events, how protein needs change in a calorie deficit, and what health problems low energy availability can cause, including the syndrome now called relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S).[8][4][9][10][11] A separate psychology literature studies how the face signals body weight and how observers judge facial adiposity for health and attractiveness.[12] Mainstream press and eating-disorder specialists have also covered the online trend, mostly in terms of risk to teenagers.[13] No trial has tested very low body fat specifically as a way to change facial appearance.
infobox: About 6 to 15 percent for performance (per Wikipedia)[1]
Cut of roughly 12 to 14 weeks before a show (per Wikipedia)[17]

paras: Body fat is divided into essential fat, which supports life and reproduction, and storage fat. Wikipedia reports that about 4 to 6 percent is generally treated as the physiological minimum for men, that women need substantially more, and that bodybuilders may briefly reach very low values for competition. It adds that university work suggests roughly 6 to 15 percent for men and 12 to 18 percent for women as athletic ranges.[1]

Body fat can be estimated several ways. Wikipedia describes DXA scans, skinfold calipers, bioelectrical impedance, underwater weighing and air-displacement plethysmography, and notes that accuracy differs by method: calipers measure only subcutaneous fat and are best for tracking change with the same operator, bioelectrical impedance is affected by hydration, and some methods overstate body fat in very lean people.[1] This matters in forum discussion because quoted percentages come from different methods and are not always comparable.

General dieting literature distinguishes moderate calorie deficits from very-low-calorie diets of roughly 200 to 800 kilocalories a day, which Wikipedia says require medical supervision, and from crash dieting, which it describes as potentially dangerous without supervision.[14] Forum members use both words for what they do, from a steady deficit to short, severe restriction, and the community term starvemaxxing refers to the harsher end of that range.[3]

Fat sits in separate compartments across the face. The buccal fat pad is a deep pad of fat in each cheek between the cheek muscles; Wikipedia reports that its volume changes between childhood and adulthood, and that surgical buccal fat removal, sometimes done to reduce cheek fullness, carries a risk of damage to facial nerve branches and the parotid duct.[15] Forum members commonly describe "hollow cheeks" as a goal and attribute differences between individuals to bone structure, such as a small jaw or flatter cheekbones, in addition to fat distribution.[6]

Psychologists have studied how observers read facial adiposity. A 2018 review by de Jager, Coetzee and Coetzee in Frontiers in Psychology reports that lower facial adiposity is generally rated as more attractive and healthier, that the relationship is often curved so that both very low and very high adiposity are judged less favourably, and that a meta-analysis of seven studies found people can estimate BMI from faces alone with a correlation of about 0.71. The review also notes sex differences: for female faces raters preferred a lower BMI for attractiveness than for health, a gap not found for male faces.[12] These studies rate photographs of faces; they are not studies of dieting.

In general terms, forum members describe leanmaxxing as a phase: a sustained deficit until a target look is reached, often followed by a maintenance or gaining phase. Threads such as "Should I hit low body fat or bulk?" show the usual decision, whether to cut first to see the face or build muscle first.[2] Some posters report that continuing to lean after abdominal definition appeared improved their face; others say that a lean face looks gaunt on them.[5][16] Another thread compares how the face looks when lean and thin versus lean and muscular.[16]

Bodybuilding contest preparation is the established model. Wikipedia describes the cycle as an off-season of gaining followed by a cutting phase that starts about 12 to 14 weeks before a show, with a larger deficit speeding fat loss but raising the risk of muscle loss, and final-days manipulation of carbohydrate and water to maximise definition.[17] The 2021 peak-week review in BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation summarises these final-week practices, and a 2015 systematic review in Sports Medicine summarises what competitive bodybuilders eat.[8][9] Reviews of boxing note that high-level male and female boxers tend toward low body fat.[18] Competitors typically hold their leanest condition only briefly around the event.

Some members combine dieting with other tools. One forum thread mentions GLP-1 medication alongside dieting for fat loss, and the looksmaxxing Wikipedia entry lists weight-loss medications among practices it groups under hardmaxxing.[2][19] Those drugs have their own entries on this wiki. Gym training, discussed in the gymmaxxing article, is the usual companion so that muscle is retained.

A related online subculture uses simple, repetitive high-protein meals. In April 2026, a Kaiser Permanente pediatrician told a US television station that some patients as young as 12 were asking about restrictive, muscle-focused diets, including one popularly called "boy kibble" (ground beef and white rice), and said such diets can lack calcium, vitamin D and fibre.[13]

Opinion on forums is split. One looksmax.org poster argues that 12 to 15 percent body fat is enough to judge facial potential and that anything leaner is "cope"; a reply argues that 10 to 12 percent is ideal and that individual fat distribution matters.[5] Others ask why their face looks fuller despite a lean body, or why they look bloated despite good cheekbones and low body fat.[6][7] A further thread lists reasons the poster does not want to go very low body fat.[20]

In February 2024 Business Insider (carried by Yahoo) reported on what it called starvemaxxing, quoting a December 2023 subreddit thread in which a user asked how many calories people eat to get hollow cheeks and a reply gave a low figure. The article reports that forum threads on hollow cheeks go back to 2018, that the looksmaxxing hashtag had more than 6 billion TikTok views and the starvemaxxing hashtag about 8 million, and that some posts described self-induced vomiting.[3]

Creators quoted in the article described the content differently. TikTok creator Kareem Shami said starvemaxxing is not literally starving but cutting to a low body fat percentage, and described much looksmaxxing content as satire; creator Johan Drumev called it mostly a joke while warning that young teenagers might take it seriously. Brazilian model Francisco Lachowski, whose look is often cited as a reference in these videos, said he was saddened that his work had influenced unhealthy behaviours.[3]

A 2014 systematic review in the International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism examined dietary protein in energy-restricted, resistance-trained lean athletes and made a case for higher intakes than in the general population.[4] The 2015 Sports Medicine review of competitive bodybuilders' diets and the 2021 peak-week review describe common competition practices and the limits of the research behind them.[8][9]

The IOC-commissioned 2013 position statement on weight-sensitive sports reviewed how to reduce health risks for athletes who must control body mass.[10] Wikipedia reports that the 1980s female athlete triad was broadened by a 2014 IOC consensus to RED-S, which covers low energy availability, disordered eating and impaired bone health, and that in men prolonged low energy availability has been linked to lower androgen levels, bone density and strength.[11]

The Minnesota Starvation Experiment is the classic study of prolonged restriction. Between November 1944 and December 1945, Ancel Keys and colleagues at the University of Minnesota studied 36 men who spent 24 weeks on roughly half their previous intake. According to Wikipedia, the men showed lower heart rate and body temperature, food preoccupation, reduced sexual interest, social withdrawal and rises in depression scores, and the rehabilitation phase was hard for many.[21] The study is cited in discussions of how restriction affects mood and behaviour, though its design and calorie targets differ from voluntary leanmaxxing.

General dieting reviews summarised on Wikipedia report that weight lost through severe restriction is often regained and that dieting can contribute to eating disorders in people with other risk factors.[14] Dietitians and body-image researchers quoted by Business Insider in 2024 raised concerns about teenagers: pediatric dietitian Clare Thornton-Wood called starvemaxxing very unwise, Elizabeth Daniels of the University of the West of England's Centre for Appearance Research said young viewers may not tell jokes from reality, and a spokesperson for the eating-disorder charity Beat said such videos could worsen eating disorders. They also said facial structure is largely genetic.[3]

High-definition liposculpture, a surgical technique for contouring fat, appears in the plastic-surgery literature as a way to emphasise muscle definition, and is sometimes mentioned alongside dieting in physique discussions.[22]

The RED-S literature reports hormonal and bone consequences, higher stress-fracture risk, fatigue, slow healing and mood problems from low energy availability, with the evidence base for men smaller than for women.[10][11] Wikipedia notes that treatment usually involves restoring energy balance under multidisciplinary care and that bone loss may not be fully reversible.[11]

Very-low-calorie dieting is described on Wikipedia as capable of causing muscle loss, gout and electrolyte disturbance.[14] Experts quoted in 2024 warned that severe restriction in teenagers risks poor bone health and growth, and that refeeding syndrome can follow a return to normal eating after very low intake.[3]

Disordered eating and body-image concerns in men and women are studied using instruments such as the Male Body Attitudes Scale and the SATAQ-4, which measures internalisation of appearance ideals.[23][24] Muscle dysmorphia, a form of body dysmorphic disorder in which people believe they are too small or insufficiently muscular, is associated on Wikipedia's summary with strict dietary regimens and higher disordered-eating scores, with onset commonly in late adolescence.[25] Eating-disorder charities advise anyone worried about their eating to seek help from a doctor.

No studies found of extreme dieting or very low body fat as a way to change facial appearance. Related research covers dietary protein during calorie restriction in lean athletes, competitor nutrition and peak-week practices, the perception of facial adiposity in photographs, the Minnesota Starvation Experiment, and IOC reviews of athlete health risks.[8][4][9][10][21][12]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org and in video content, going lean is treated as a core step for facial definition, with threads debating how low is enough, why some faces stay full, and whether very low body fat is worth it.[5][6][20]

claims.claim: About 10 to 12% body fat is ideal for the face
Under 12 to 15% body fat is 'cope' for judging your face

Starvemaxxing is mostly a joke or satire

Simple high-protein diets such as ground beef and rice maximise muscle
